title: Query Plans and Cardinality Lab
description: Inspect SQL query plans, join choices, cardinality errors, searchable predicates, and reproducible benchmarks while preserving exact result semantics.

questions.question_text: What does query optimization choose?
options: A physical way to produce the required result
questions.explanation: Optimization selects execution alternatives while preserving semantics.

questions.question_text: Which must be established before timing a rewrite?
questions.explanation: A fast wrong answer is not an improvement.

questions.question_text: What can stale statistics affect?
options: The meaning of primary key uniqueness
questions.explanation: Statistics inform estimated distributions and row counts.

questions.question_text: Why test a popular course as well as a rare course?
options: Popular courses always have NULL IDs
Data skew can change work substantially
questions.explanation: Different selectivities can expose different workload behavior.

questions.question_text: When can a nested loop be efficient?
options: A small outer input with selective inner lookups
Only when there are no indexes
questions.explanation: Low iteration counts and cheap lookups can make loops effective.

questions.question_text: What is a hash join conceptually doing?
options: Building a key lookup and probing it
questions.explanation: Hashing supports matching keys across inputs.

questions.question_text: Is every textbook join algorithm available in every engine?
questions.explanation: Capabilities depend on engine and version.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes EXPLAIN ANALYZE from ordinary EXPLAIN in this MySQL context?
questions.explanation: Runtime analysis entails execution rather than estimates alone.

questions.question_text: Why trace the first estimate divergence?
options: Earlier errors can amplify later work
All errors start in ORDER BY
A divergent estimate proves bad SQL syntax
questions.explanation: Downstream choices can reflect an earlier cardinality mistake.

questions.question_text: Which predicate directly expresses February 2026 for a DATE column?
questions.explanation: The half open interval includes exactly the requested date range.

questions.question_text: What can a join on nonunique course titles cause?
questions.explanation: Shared labels can create multiple matches.

questions.question_text: Does an existing index guarantee optimizer use?
options: Only if its name is short
questions.explanation: The optimizer evaluates available alternatives and costs.

questions.question_text: What is a reproducible benchmark record missing if parameters are omitted?
questions.explanation: Parameter values can materially change the work.

questions.question_text: Why separate warm and initial cache observations?
options: Cache state changes measured I/O work
Warm data always returns different rows
questions.explanation: Caching can change runtime without changing semantics.

questions.question_text: What should an optimization report include besides read benefit?
questions.explanation: Indexes can shift costs to writes and maintenance.

questions.question_text: What is sargability concerned with?
options: Mapping predicates to useful search conditions
questions.explanation: Searchable conditions can support suitable access paths.

questions.question_text: Can function predicates ever use indexes?
options: Yes, with suitable structures or supported rewrites
questions.explanation: Expression indexes and optimizer capabilities are relevant.

questions.question_text: What makes a tiny fixture insufficient for throughput claims?
options: It lacks representative scale and distribution
questions.explanation: Logical correctness and production performance need different evidence.

questions.question_text: Why avoid clearing a shared production cache for a casual benchmark?
options: It disrupts other workload and changes operational conditions
questions.explanation: A controlled test must respect shared system impact.

questions.question_text: What is the correct conclusion from a reasoned sample result?
options: It proves every index is optimal
It proves the provider executed SQL
It predicts semantics, not an observed plan or timing
questions.explanation: Static examples do not constitute runtime evidence.

notes:
## Separate a correct answer from a good access plan

A course dashboard counts paid registrations in a date interval. The SQL can be logically correct while reading far more rows than expected. Query optimization chooses among physical ways to produce the same required result. It considers scans, indexes, join methods, filtering, and intermediate results. The useful question is not whether an index exists, but whether the selected plan performs suitable work for the actual data distribution and requested result.

Start with correctness before performance. Define one registration row, the eligibility condition, the time boundary, and the grouping grain. Include duplicate payments and missing optional fields in reasoning. A rewrite that becomes fast by dropping legitimate rows is a regression. Keep the original result contract and compare outputs while investigating access costs. Timing alone cannot tell whether a faster query answers the same question.

## Build a bounded investigation

The teaching fixture separates courses from registrations. Course identifiers are unique, while many registrations can refer to one course. The date index is a candidate access path rather than a guarantee about the chosen plan. Use integer fee units to keep the result arithmetic exact in this small example.

```sql
CREATE TABLE courses (
 course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE registrations (
 registration_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 course_id INT NOT NULL,
 paid_on DATE NOT NULL,
 fee INT NOT NULL,
 INDEX ix_paid_course (paid_on,course_id)
);
INSERT INTO courses VALUES (10,'Databases'),(20,'Networks');
INSERT INTO registrations VALUES
 (1,10,'2026-02-01',100),(2,10,'2026-02-08',100),
 (3,20,'2026-03-01',200);
SELECT c.course_id,SUM(r.fee) AS total
FROM courses c JOIN registrations r ON r.course_id=c.course_id
WHERE r.paid_on >= '2026-02-01' AND r.paid_on < '2026-03-01'
GROUP BY c.course_id ORDER BY c.course_id;
```

The expected result is course 10 with total 200. The March row is outside the half open interval. This fixture checks semantics; three rows cannot establish production throughput. Keep a separate representative performance fixture with recorded scale and distribution. Avoid using private production rows merely to obtain realistic looking examples.

## Estimate rows and inspect actual rows

An optimizer estimates how many rows pass filters and joins. Statistics summarize data distribution and help those estimates. An estimate can be wrong when values are skewed, columns are correlated, or statistics no longer reflect changed data. If most registrations belong to one very popular course, assuming a uniform distribution can misrepresent the work for that course.

Compare estimates at the point where row counts first diverge from execution evidence. A mistaken early filter estimate can influence join order and multiply downstream work. Do not blame only the final sort because it is visibly slow. Trace how many rows reach that sort and why. Refreshing statistics can help some cases, but it is not a universal repair for an unsuitable predicate, missing relationship constraint, or impossible selectivity assumption.

Record the query parameters with a plan. The same SQL text can behave differently for a rare course and a popular one. A benchmark using only the most selective parameter may conceal the production hotspot. Include common, rare, empty, and boundary inputs. Distinguish expected workload variability from a reproducible regression under the same conditions.

## Understand join methods as physical alternatives

A nested loop conceptually takes rows from one input and finds matches in another. An indexed lookup can make that efficient when the outer input is small and the inner search is selective. Repeating an expensive inner scan for many outer rows can be costly. The loop itself is not inherently bad; the number of iterations and the work in each iteration matter.

A hash join builds a lookup structure from one input and probes it with another under supported join conditions. Memory requirements and spilling can matter when inputs are large. A merge join, available in some engines, consumes compatibly ordered inputs and advances through matching keys. These are conceptual algorithms; their availability and detailed variants depend on the installed database version. Do not assume MySQL offers every algorithm described in a general textbook.

Join order can change intermediate cardinality without changing the logical result for valid equivalent transformations. A selective filter applied early can reduce work, while an unintended many to many join can explode rows. First inspect join keys and uniqueness. Adding an index to a wrong join may make a wrong result faster while leaving its multiplicity bug intact.

## EXPLAIN is different from executing analysis

In MySQL, EXPLAIN describes the optimizer's proposed plan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement it supports and reports runtime details. That distinction matters for resource use, locks, and side effects of expressions or other supported statement forms. Do not run an executing diagnostic on a sensitive workload merely because its name begins with EXPLAIN. Review the exact statement and choose an appropriate environment.

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT registration_id
FROM registrations
WHERE paid_on >= '2026-02-01' AND paid_on < '2026-03-01';
```

Inspect candidate indexes, chosen access, estimated rows, and relevant extra details in the output format used by the installed version. No plan output is fabricated in these notes. The worked solution is a method for reading the real output: identify each table access, match its filter to the query, then compare the predicted work with separate authorized execution evidence.

## Keep predicates searchable

A sargable predicate can be mapped into a useful search condition on an access structure. A direct date range often expresses a month more usefully for an ordinary date index than wrapping every date in MONTH and YEAR. This is not a rule that all functions forbid all indexing: expression indexes and optimizer rewrites can change the available choices. Match the actual predicate and installed capabilities.

Do not change timestamp semantics during a rewrite. A reporting month can depend on timezone, and a DATE example does not settle that policy. Preserve NULL behavior too: replacing a nullable comparison with a default may admit previously excluded rows. The required result contract is the baseline for every optimization experiment.

## Preserve outer join meaning during rewrites

Moving a condition from an outer join condition into WHERE can remove unmatched rows. A report requiring every course, including courses without payments, needs deliberate treatment of that distinction. An optimizer may transform expressions only when the transformation is valid under its rules; a human rewrite must meet the same semantic obligation. Test a course with no registrations before comparing performance. Also test two equal fees on distinct registrations so an accidental DISTINCT does not reduce the total. These counterexamples are small, but they protect the meaning that a large benchmark can easily obscure.

## Worked lab: find the first cardinality error

Imagine a plan estimates ten eligible registrations but execution observes ten thousand. The solution begins at the date filter or course distribution, rather than immediately forcing a different join method. Check the exact interval, parameter values, statistics, and distribution. Then inspect how the larger input affects subsequent loops and sorting. State what evidence would distinguish stale statistics from an inherently skewed workload.

A second counterexample is a join on title instead of course_id. Two courses can share a title, so registrations can multiply. The correct repair is the identity join. A row count comparison and deliberate duplicate title fixture expose this semantic error before physical tuning begins. Explain why a unique identifier relationship matters to both correct results and plausible cardinality estimates.

## Worked lab: benchmark a range rewrite

Compare the original month extraction predicate with the direct half open range on the same dataset. First verify equal results across the month boundary and empty intervals. Then record plans, runtime observations, rows examined when available, engine version, table scale, indexes, and parameter values. Separate warm cache repetitions from initial reads and record concurrent workload conditions. Avoid clearing a shared production cache to make a benchmark look controlled.

Repeat enough times to see variability, and report the observations rather than a universal speedup claim. Include the cost of maintaining any new index during writes. A query improvement can still be a poor system tradeoff when it makes a high volume write path unacceptable. This foundation covers the inspection process; the physical experiments and production rollout remain separate tasks.

Read [Clustered Index](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/clustered-index) and [Function Based Index Concept](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/function-based-index-concept) for specific access structures. These solved plan and benchmark labs cannot be graded meaningfully by SELECT output alone, so no result-only coding task is substituted for physical evidence.
